subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Stringing Symmetry — Two Colours, One Necklace

tasks_in_class.description: Colour the beads in the strings using two colours to show the malas that you have made (4 beads of one colour, 4 of another).
On the previous page, tick the malas that are symmetrical.
Tick the malas that are symmetrical and cross the one(s) that are not symmetrical from the given bead-string pictures.

homework.description: Use 6 beads of one colour and 2 beads of another colour to make symmetrical malas.

time_bands.activity: Children receive bead outlines (or draw their own string of 8 circles). They colour 4 beads in one colour and 4 in a second colour, making several different arrangements — Let us Do Q1, p.178 ("Colour the beads using two colours to show malas..."). Pairs compare their completed strings and informally describe what they notice.

The class folds one of their coloured strings in half (or imagines the fold) and asks: do both halves look the same? This concrete check introduces the word symmetrical. Children then work on Let us Do Q2, p.179 ("tick the malas that are symmetrical") and Let us Do Q3a, p.179 ("tick the symmetrical malas and cross the non-symmetrical ones from given pictures"), explaining their reasoning to a partner before marking.

A quick count-round: each child holds up one string and the class gives a thumbs-up (symmetrical) or thumbs-down (not symmetrical), with one child stating why. The teacher surfaces the pattern: a mala is symmetrical when both halves are exactly the same. Additional practice from the same page is noted for take-home — Let us Do Q3b, p.179 ("use 6 and 2 beads of two colours to make symmetrical malas").

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have coloured bead strings can physically fold the paper to check — this concrete fold-and-check is the anchor for the word 'symmetrical.' A common error is thinking that any split of the 8 beads into two halves makes the mala symmetrical; ask children to show that the left half and right half must look the same bead-for-bead. Let us Do Q3b is routed as take-home so children explore the 6+2 combination at their own pace.
materials: Printed or drawn bead-string outlines (8 circles per string)
Crayons or coloured pencils (at least two contrasting colours)

periods.activity_title: Fold, Trace, and Find the Line — Rangoli Symmetry

tasks_in_class.description: Observe the rangolis given below. Are all rangolis symmetrical?
Trace these rangolis on a paper. Fold the tracing paper in such a way that one half of the rangoli lies exactly on the other half.
Draw lines in the given rangolis that divide them into two identical halves.
Look for other symmetrical things around you. Discuss.

time_bands.activity: Children open to p.180 and observe the kolam, Pookalam, and Aipan rangolis. They answer Let us Think Q1, p.180 ("Are all rangolis symmetrical?") first individually, then share with a partner. The teacher collects a show of hands for yes/no before revealing that not all rangolis are symmetrical — this discrepancy drives the investigation.

Children place tracing paper over the rangolis for Let us Think Q2, p.180 ("trace and fold so one half lies exactly on the other"). They fold along their chosen line and hold the folded tracing paper up to the light to see whether both layers align. Pairs who disagree on where to fold negotiate and re-try.

Children draw the lines of symmetry directly in the rangoli pictures on p.180 — Let us Think Q3, p.180 ("draw lines that divide the rangolis into two identical halves"). The teacher circulates, prompting: 'If you folded along that line, would both halves match exactly?'

A brief hunt: Let us Think Q4, p.180 ("look for symmetrical things around you — discuss"). Children name two objects in the classroom or on their body (e.g. a window, their face) and the class evaluates. The teacher draws together the shared principle: a line of symmetry divides a shape into two halves that are mirror images of each other.

periods.teacher_notes: The unit builds on the bead-string symmetry work where children compared two halves of a mala; rangolis extend that idea to more complex shapes with multiple possible lines of symmetry. A common error is drawing a diagonal line through a rangoli and assuming it is always a line of symmetry — the fold test exposes this quickly. Additional rangoli completion work (Let us Do Q1–Q2, p.181) can follow if time permits, or serve as paired classwork in the next available sitting.

periods.activity_title: Complete the Rangoli — Drawing the Missing Half

tasks_in_class.description: Draw and complete the symmetrical rangolis given below (three rangoli patterns — (a), (b), (c) — with one half provided).
Draw some more rangolis in your notebook that are symmetrical.

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a large half-shape on the board and asks a volunteer to complete the missing half symmetrically. The class discusses: what questions do you ask yourself as you draw each dot? This surfaces the strategy of mirroring each point at the same distance from the line of symmetry.

Children work through Let us Do Q1, p.181 ("draw and complete the symmetrical rangolis — (a), (b), (c) — with one half provided"). Each child completes all three patterns independently. The teacher circulates and asks: 'How did you decide where to put the next dot?' Children who finish quickly compare their completion with a partner and identify any differences.

Children attempt Let us Do Q2, p.181 ("draw some more rangolis in your notebook that are symmetrical") — an unhurried making activity where children invent their own symmetrical designs on dot paper or in notebooks. Two or three children briefly share their designs; the class traces the line of symmetry with a finger before deciding whether it is symmetrical.

periods.teacher_notes: The line-of-symmetry and fold concepts explored with rangoli patterns on p.180 now carry forward into constructing the missing half; children who struggled with identifying the line will benefit from counting squares or dots from the fold line on each side. A common error is reflecting the half correctly but forgetting to mirror the colouring as well — prompt children to check colour as well as shape. Let us Do Q2 is deliberately open-ended and can be extended or taken into notebooks.

periods.activity_title: Fold, Cut, Reveal — Making a Symmetrical Cat Mask

tasks_in_class.description: Fold paper along the middle, draw half a cat, cut it out, open the fold, make eyes and nose, colour it and attach a rubber band — your symmetrical cat mask is ready.
What is the trick the painter is playing? Find things for the painter to draw so that he can no longer play the trick. Draw three such things here.

time_bands.activity: Each child receives a sheet of paper, folds it in half, and draws half a cat face on one side — following the Make Masks activity, p.182. They cut through both layers, unfold, add eye and nose holes, colour symmetrically, and attach a rubber band. As children hold up their masks, the teacher compares a well-aligned mask (like Soni's) with a deliberately misaligned one to show what non-symmetry feels like when worn.

The teacher reads or narrates the Tit for Tat story (p.183). The class discusses: what trick is the painter playing, and why does it only work for symmetrical objects? Children name two or three examples of objects where the mirror trick would work (e.g. a leaf, a face) and one where it would not (e.g. a hand).

Children work individually on Let us Think Q1, p.183 ("find things for the painter to draw so that he can no longer play the trick — draw three such things"). They share with a partner and decide together: is each object truly non-symmetrical? The teacher invites one or two pairs to justify their choices to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The mask-making embeds the fold-and-reveal process that children used with tracing paper on rangolis; the cut mask makes symmetry tangible and immediate. A common error in the Tit for Tat task is selecting objects that are actually symmetrical — encourage children to check by imagining a fold down the middle and asking whether both sides would look the same. Materials for mask-making must be available at the start of this unit.
materials: A4 or square paper sheets (one per child)

periods.activity_title: Counter by Counter — Playing the Mirror Game

tasks_in_class.description: Play the mirror game: one player places four counters on their side of the grid; the other places counters on their side as the mirror image. Switch roles and repeat.
Has Avi placed the counters at the right places? Check it by placing the mirror on the line drawn.

time_bands.activity: The teacher sets up the 4×4 grid on the board (or chalks one on the floor) with a clear centre mirror line. The teacher places two counters on the left side and asks: where should they go on the right side to be a mirror image? A volunteer tries; the class verifies with the physical mirror held along the line.

Pairs open to p.184 and play The Mirror Game: one partner places four counters on their half of the grid; the other places counters on their half as the mirror image. After each round they hold the mirror along the line to check — The Mirror Game, p.184 ("one player places four counters; the other places counters as the mirror image; switch roles and repeat"). Pairs switch roles after each successful round.

Children study the verification question on p.184 — The Mirror Game (verification), p.184 ("has Avi placed the counters correctly? — check by placing the mirror on the line"). They write or say whether Avi's placement is correct and why. The class debriefs: what is the rule for placing a counter on the mirror-image side? (Same row, but on the opposite side at the same distance from the line.)

periods.teacher_notes: The mirror game puts the reflection concept from mask-making and rangoli folding into a dynamic, two-player spatial context. A common error is placing counters in the correct column but the wrong row — remind children that the mirror line is vertical, so row position stays the same while the column flips. Ensure each pair has a small mirror strip or a reflective ruler; if mirrors are short, pairs can share one between two groups.
materials: Small mirrors or reflective strips (one per pair)
Counters or small coins in two colours (eight per pair)
4×4 grid drawn on paper or chalk on the floor

periods.activity_title: Odd One Out and Mirror Grids — Pushing Symmetry Thinking

tasks_in_class.description: Pick the odd one out and give reasons (from four pairs of shape-and-dot arrangements).
Fill 4 boxes with red colour and 3 with blue colour in such a way that one side is the mirror image of the other. In how many ways can you fill it?
Make Micy's side the same as that of Catty's side. You can rearrange only three balls in Micy's side.

homework.description: Which shape cutouts would fit in the given hexagon shape without overlapping and gaps?

time_bands.activity: Children work on Let us Explore Q1, p.185 ("pick the odd one out and give reasons from four pairs of shape-and-dot arrangements"). They work individually first, then share reasons with a partner. The teacher invites two children with different choices to explain, using the language of symmetry.

Children tackle Let us Explore Q2, p.185 ("fill 4 boxes red and 3 blue so one side is the mirror image of the other — in how many ways?"). They try one solution first, then systematically look for others. Pairs compare their solutions and decide whether they have found all possible arrangements.

Children work on Let us Explore Q3, p.185 ("make Micy's side the same as Catty's side by rearranging only three balls"). They use trial and reasoning to find which three balls to move. Let us Explore Q4, p.185 is noted as take-home work for those who wish to extend — children look at the hexagon puzzle and make a prediction before leaving.

periods.teacher_notes: These tasks require children to move beyond visual identification of symmetry into reasoning about why an arrangement is or is not symmetric, and into systematic thinking about how many solutions exist. A common error in Q2 is colouring arrangements that look balanced but are not strict mirror images — prompt children to fold the page mentally along the mirror line and check each cell. Q4 is routed as take-home to allow unhurried shape exploration.

periods.activity_title: Fill Without Gaps — Rangometry Shapes and Tessellating Paths

tasks_in_class.description: Use rangometry shapes to fill the given shapes (rectangle, square, hexagon) with no gaps and overlaps.
Use two or more rangometry shapes to create your tiles. Now, trace the tiles to create different paths.
Try making these paths (three given tessellation patterns using repeated tiles).

time_bands.activity: The teacher tells the story of grandpa's foot stuck in a gap between tiles, then holds up a square tile and asks: if we tile a floor with these, will there be any gaps? Children predict, then the teacher slides two squares together to show no gap. The puzzle: does every shape tile without gaps?

Children use rangometry shapes (triangles, squares, rhombuses, trapezoids) to fill the outlines in their textbook — Let us Do Q1, p.186 ("fill the rectangle, square, and hexagon with no gaps and overlaps"). They try each shape and record which ones work. Pairs share what they discovered.

Children join two or more rangometry shapes to form a composite tile — Let us Do Q1, p.187 ("use two or more shapes to create your tile; trace it to create different paths"). They trace their composite tile repeatedly on paper to build a path, discovering that the repeated tracing produces a regular pattern.

Children attempt Let us Do Q2, p.187 ("try making these three given tessellation paths"). They choose one of the three patterns and try to reproduce it with their shapes. The teacher circulates and asks: what do you notice about where the edges of each tile meet?

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds on the pattern-recognition work done with rangolis; tessellation is a spatial cousin of symmetry — a shape tiles without gaps when its edges align perfectly with copies of itself. A common error is placing shapes so they partially overlap rather than edge-to-edge — remind children to slide, not stack, each shape up against the last. Rangometry shape sets should be available before the unit begins; if sets are limited, pairs may share.
materials: Rangometry shape sets (one per pair or shared)

section_titles: Giant Wheel — Reading the Fair Map
periods.activity_title: Reading the Map — Finding Your Way at the Fair

tasks_in_class.description: Imagine sitting with Soni and Avi. Think of a place or stall, and challenge your friend to find out which stall you have in mind. Help them guess by answering yes or no.
How many exit routes are there in the fair?
Follow the path Avi and Soni are following: walk on blue lane, turn right on green lane, take left towards red lane, take first left on golden lane, pass stalls to find the chaupal.
An uncle asks Dada ji the way to the ATM. Tell him the way to the ATM from the chaupal.

homework.description: Which place does the chaupal sign show?

time_bands.activity: Children open to the Surajkund fair map (p.188–189). The teacher walks through the legend together: each symbol is named and children point to an example on the map. Children then play Let us Play, p.188 ("think of a stall and challenge your friend to guess it using yes or no answers") with a partner — this forces close reading of the map and symbol meanings.

Children answer Let us Do Q1d, p.190 ("how many exit routes are there in the fair?") by counting and marking exits on the map. The teacher consolidates: symbols let a map give a lot of information without words.

Children trace the multi-step route in Let us Do Q2, p.190 ("walk on blue lane, turn right on green lane, take left on red lane, take first left on golden lane, pass stalls to reach the chaupal") with a finger on the map first, then mark it with a pencil. Pairs compare their traced routes.

Children write or say the directions for Let us Do Q3, p.190 ("tell an uncle the way to the ATM from the chaupal"), using the direction words left, right, and forward. Two or three children share their directions and the class follows them on the map to verify.

periods.teacher_notes: Map reading is new spatial vocabulary — children moving from symmetry and tiling to navigation need time to decode the legend before tackling route questions. A common error is confusing left and right when the figure on the map faces a different direction to the reader; encourage children to turn their book or imagine walking into the map. The three symbol-identification questions (Q1a, Q1b, Q1c) are straightforward look-up tasks and are grouped for take-home so in-class time prioritises route-following.

section_titles: Giant Wheel — Reading the Fair Map
periods.activity_title: Through the Maze — Navigating Out of the Fair

tasks_in_class.description: Circle the picture in the map that shows the play area.
Which place does the parking sign show?
Follow the maze with Soni and Avi to exit the fair.
Share the way you went through the maze. Write the things you found on the way.

time_bands.activity: Children complete the two remaining symbol-identification tasks from the fair map: Let us Do Q1b, p.190 ("circle the picture that shows the play area") and Let us Do Q1c, p.190 ("which place does the parking sign show?"). These quick tasks consolidate legend-reading skills built in the map unit, then the class moves on to the exit scenario.

The teacher sets the scene: the fair day is over and Soni and Avi need to find the exit. Children turn to p.191 and navigate Let us Do Q1, p.191 ("follow the maze with Soni and Avi to exit the fair") — tracing a route with a pencil. Children who reach an exit early can try the other possible exit, comparing which path is shorter.

Children write their maze path for Let us Do Q2, p.191 ("share the way you went — write the things you found on the way"). They note objects encountered (snake, dog, pineapple, kite, star) in order and describe their turns in directional words. Two or three children read their descriptions aloud while the class follows on the page to check.

periods.teacher_notes: The maze brings together the directional language (left, right, forward) practised in map-reading and wraps it in a playful problem-solving context; children who took different paths through the maze will encounter different objects, making the writing task genuinely varied. A common error is skipping objects along the route — encourage children to trace slowly and list each object they pass. The two symbol tasks at the start are brief closure items from the map section and free the bulk of the unit for maze exploration.

section_titles: Giant Wheel — Reading the Fair Map
periods.activity_title: The Surajkund Fair — Symmetry, Tiles, and Maps Come Together

time_bands.activity: Children receive a sheet with six simple shapes (a leaf, a jug, a letter P, a plain rectangle, a star, a hand). Working in pairs, they sort the shapes into two groups: symmetrical and not symmetrical. Each pair must give one reason for each decision, using the vocabulary fold, line of symmetry, and mirror image built across the chapter's symmetry work.

Pairs receive a blank 4×4 grid divided by a vertical line. One partner colours four cells on their half; the other must colour the mirror image on their half — drawing on the counter-placement and mirror-line reasoning from the mirror game and the symmetry puzzle work. They swap roles and repeat with a new arrangement. A small mirror strip is available for self-checking.

Children use two or three rangometry shapes (or cut paper squares and triangles) to create a composite tile, trace it three or four times in a row to make a short path, and decide: does their path tile without gaps? They label their design with the names of the shapes they used, connecting to the tessellation discoveries from the tiling section.

A mini-fair map challenge: the teacher draws a simple 6-place sketch map on the board (entrance, pond, stall, exit, ATM, chaupal) with three labelled paths. Children write two sentences giving directions from the entrance to the chaupal using the directional words from the fair map and maze sections. Volunteers share; the class traces the route on the board to verify.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together every major idea of the chapter — symmetry of malas, rangolis, masks, and mirror grids; tessellating tiles; and map-based navigation — into four connected activities that the children complete independently. The sorting task and mirror-grid task revisit reflection symmetry in paired work; the tile path connects symmetry to tessellation; and the mini-map connects spatial reasoning to directional language. No materials from earlier units are needed; everything is produced fresh within these minutes.
materials: Shape-sorting sheets (six shapes per pair, printed or hand-drawn)
Blank 4×4 grid sheets divided by a centre line (one per pair)
Rangometry shapes or cut paper squares and triangles
Notebooks or plain paper for tile tracing and map directions

items.prompt: A bead necklace has 8 beads: some red and some blue. Which arrangement makes the necklace symmetrical?

options.label: A
options.text: Red, Red, Red, Blue, Red, Blue, Blue, Blue

options.label: B
options.text: Red, Blue, Red, Blue, Blue, Red, Blue, Red

options.label: C
options.text: Red, Blue, Blue, Red, Red, Blue, Blue, Red

options.label: D
options.text: Blue, Blue, Blue, Blue, Red, Red, Red, Blue

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — Red, Blue, Blue, Red, Red, Blue, Blue, Red. The first half (Red, Blue, Blue, Red) is the same as the second half, making both halves identical.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the string in half and check whether both halves show the same bead colours in the same order.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may not be checking whether both halves are the same; this arrangement has unequal colour groups and the halves differ.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may be thinking of alternating colours rather than checking that the two halves are identical when folded.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may be choosing an arrangement with a colour pattern without verifying that folding the necklace in half produces matching halves.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child colour eight circles and physically fold the paper in half to compare; stretch: ask them to make a different symmetrical arrangement with 4 red and 4 blue beads.

exercise.description: Colour the beads in the strings using two colours to show the malas that you have made (4 beads of one colour, 4 of another).

items.prompt: Look at the half-rangoli below. Draw the missing half to complete the symmetrical rangoli. The line down the middle is the line of symmetry.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The completed rangoli is a mirror image of the given half: each dot, line, or petal on the left side appears at the same distance and position on the right side of the line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: For each point on the given half, count the same number of units across the line of symmetry and place the matching point on the other side.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use a mirror held along the centre line to see the reflected half before drawing; stretch: ask them to draw a rangoli of their own design and mark its line of symmetry.

exercise.description: Draw and complete the symmetrical rangolis given below (three rangoli patterns — (a), (b), (c) — with one half provided).

items.prompt: Priya wants to make a symmetrical mask. She folds a sheet of paper in half and draws half the mask on one side. What should she do next to get a symmetrical mask?

options.label: A
options.text: Unfold the paper and draw the other half freehand from memory.

options.label: B
options.text: Cut through both layers along the drawing, then unfold.

options.label: C
options.text: Cut only the top layer, then draw the other half on the bottom layer.

options.label: D
options.text: Trace the half onto a new sheet and place the two sheets side by side.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Cut through both layers along the drawn outline, then unfold. Because both layers are cut together along the fold, the two halves are identical, producing a symmetrical mask.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Cutting through both folded layers at once ensures both halves are the same shape, giving a symmetrical result when unfolded.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child understands folding but misses that cutting through both layers is what creates matching halves; drawing freehand risks making the halves different.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child confuses cutting one layer with cutting both; only cutting through both layers at once guarantees symmetry.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child treats the two halves as separate pieces rather than understanding that the fold makes them identical when cut together.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child actually fold, draw, and cut a piece of paper to see the result; stretch: ask them to make a mask with two lines of symmetry and explain why that is or is not possible.

exercise.description: Fold paper along the middle, draw half a cat, cut it out, open the fold, make eyes and nose, colour it and attach a rubber band — your symmetrical cat mask is ready.

items.prompt: In the mirror game, a 4×4 grid is divided by a vertical line in the middle. Riya places a counter in the top-left corner of her half. Where should Dev place his counter on his half to make a correct mirror image? Describe the position.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Dev should place his counter in the top-right corner of his half — which is in the same row (top row) as Riya's counter, in the cell immediately to the right of the mirror line, matching the same distance from the line as Riya's counter.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Keep the row the same and place the counter the same number of cells away from the mirror line on the opposite side.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use a physical mirror held along the centre line so the child can see where the reflection lands; stretch: ask the child to place three counters and have a partner create the full mirror image without using the mirror to check first.

exercise.description: Play the mirror game: one player places four counters on their side of the grid; the other places counters on their side as the mirror image. Switch roles and repeat.

items.prompt: Ravi uses square tiles to cover a flat surface. Which statement is true about squares used as tiles?

options.label: A
options.text: Squares leave triangular gaps at every corner.

options.label: B
options.text: Squares fit together with no gaps and no overlaps.

options.label: C
options.text: Squares can only tile a circle shape.

options.label: D
options.text: Squares always need another shape to fill the gaps.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Squares fit together with no gaps and no overlaps. Their straight sides and right-angle corners mean every edge aligns perfectly with the next square.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place square tiles edge-to-edge; because all sides are equal and corners are right angles, no gap is left.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may be confusing squares with circles or curved shapes that do leave gaps; squares have straight sides that align.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may be thinking of shapes that fit only specific outlines; squares tile any rectangular region and many others.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may be confusing squares with irregular shapes or pentagons; squares tessellate on their own without a helper shape.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child place four square cut-outs on a table and see that no gap forms; stretch: ask whether a regular pentagon would tile the same way and why.

exercise.description: Use rangometry shapes to fill the given shapes (rectangle, square, hexagon) with no gaps and overlaps.

items.prompt: Imagine you are walking through a maze. You start at the entrance, go straight, then turn left, walk a little, then turn right, and reach the exit. Write down three turns or directions you used on your path.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A correct answer names three directional moves from the description: (1) go straight, (2) turn left, (3) turn right. Any response that lists three distinct direction words from this path in order is acceptable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall each move in order and name the direction word (straight, left, right) for each step.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child act out the path physically in the classroom, then name what they did; stretch: ask them to write a full description of a different path through the maze including all the objects they would pass.

exercise.description: Follow the maze with Soni and Avi to exit the fair.

items.prompt: A necklace has this bead order: Green, Yellow, Yellow, Green, Green, Yellow, Green, Yellow. Is this necklace symmetrical? Choose the correct reason.

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because it uses only two colours.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because it has 8 beads in total.

options.label: C
options.text: No, because the first half (Green, Yellow, Yellow, Green) is different from the second half (Green, Yellow, Green, Yellow).

options.label: D
options.text: No, because green beads are more than yellow beads.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — The necklace is not symmetrical because the first half (Green, Yellow, Yellow, Green) does not match the second half (Green, Yellow, Green, Yellow) when the string is folded in the middle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split the 8-bead string into two halves of 4 and compare each position: position 1 vs position 8, position 2 vs position 7, and so on.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child confuses the number of colours used with the symmetry of arrangement; using two colours does not guarantee symmetry.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child thinks total bead count determines symmetry; symmetry depends on whether both halves match, not on the count alone.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child is comparing quantities of each colour rather than checking whether the arrangement of beads mirrors across the fold.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child write the 8 bead colours in a row, draw a line after the 4th bead, and compare pairs (1st with 8th, 2nd with 7th); stretch: ask them to change the minimum number of beads to make this necklace symmetrical.

exercise.description: On the previous page, tick the malas that are symmetrical.

items.prompt: Meena says: 'Every rangoli must be symmetrical because rangolis are beautiful patterns.' Do you agree? Give one reason for your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No, not every rangoli is symmetrical. A rangoli can be a beautiful pattern even if its two halves are not identical. Symmetry requires that one half is an exact mirror image of the other, and not all rangoli designs meet this condition.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check by imagining a fold: if both halves would lie exactly on each other, the rangoli is symmetrical; if not, it is not — beauty and symmetry are different things.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the child two rangoli outlines — one symmetrical, one not — and ask which would fold to match; stretch: ask the child to describe a rangoli that is beautiful but has no line of symmetry.

exercise.description: Observe the rangolis given below. Are all rangolis symmetrical?

items.prompt: The painter draws only half a picture and uses a mirror to show the full image. For which object would this trick NOT work?

options.label: A
options.text: A butterfly

options.label: B
options.text: A human face looking straight ahead

options.label: C
options.text: A right hand

options.label: D
options.text: A symmetrical leaf

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — A right hand. The mirror image of a right hand is a left hand, not another right hand, so using a mirror to complete the picture would give the wrong object.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The trick works only for symmetrical objects; a hand is not symmetrical because its mirror image is the opposite hand.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may be thinking of the irregular wing patterns of some butterflies; a typical butterfly outline has a vertical line of symmetry, so the trick works.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may be unsure about faces; a face seen from the front has an approximate vertical line of symmetry, so the mirror trick works reasonably well.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may be confusing irregular leaves with the symmetrical leaf shape intended; a symmetrical leaf has a midrib line of symmetry, so the trick works.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace their right hand and then hold the tracing in front of a mirror — they will see the reflected image is a left hand; stretch: ask them to find two more objects at home that would defeat the painter's trick and explain why.

exercise.description: What is the trick the painter is playing? Find things for the painter to draw so that he can no longer play the trick. Draw three such things here.

items.prompt: In the mirror game, Avi places a counter in Row 2, Column 1 of his half (the left half of a 4×4 grid). The mirror line is between Column 2 and Column 3. Where must Soni place her counter on the right half to make a correct mirror image?

options.label: A
options.text: Row 2, Column 3

options.label: B
options.text: Row 1, Column 3

options.label: C
options.text: Row 2, Column 4

options.label: D
options.text: Row 3, Column 3

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — Row 2, Column 3. Avi's counter is in Row 2, Column 1, which is 2 columns to the left of the mirror line. The mirror image is 2 columns to the right of the mirror line, which is Column 3, same row.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Keep the row the same; count how many columns Avi's counter is from the mirror line and place Soni's counter the same distance on the right side.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child has the correct column but has shifted the row, confusing vertical with horizontal reflection.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has moved to the correct side but placed the counter one column too far, not counting distance from the mirror line accurately.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has moved the row and placed the counter in the wrong position, showing confusion about which axis the mirror line runs along.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a printed 4×4 grid and a mirror strip; let them place a counter and hold the mirror along the centre line to find the reflection; stretch: ask the child to place two counters simultaneously and have a partner find both mirror positions.

exercise.description: Has Avi placed the counters at the right places? Check it by placing the mirror on the line drawn.

items.prompt: A grid is divided into two halves by a mirror line. You must colour 4 cells red and 3 cells blue on the left half so that the right half is the mirror image. Tanvi says there is only one way to do this. Is she right? Explain your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Tanvi is not right. There is more than one way to arrange 4 red and 3 blue cells on the left half so that the right half is its mirror image. Any valid arrangement on the left half automatically determines the right half, so different colour placements on the left give different valid solutions.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Try placing the 4 red cells in different positions on the left half; each different arrangement gives a new valid mirror-image solution, showing that multiple solutions exist.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child colour one solution, then ask 'what happens if you swap one red and one blue cell?' to prompt a second solution; stretch: ask the child to find and record as many different valid arrangements as they can, working systematically.

exercise.description: Fill 4 boxes with red colour and 3 with blue colour in such a way that one side is the mirror image of the other. In how many ways can you fill it?

items.section_title: Giant Wheel — Reading the Fair Map
items.prompt: Look at the directions below for walking from the entry gate to the pond at a fair: walk straight on the blue path, then turn right on the green path, then turn left and walk until you reach the pond. A friend joins you at the green path after your right turn. Describe the directions your friend needs from that point to reach the pond.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: From the green path (after the right turn), turn left and walk straight until you reach the pond.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Start from the point where the friend joins and trace only the remaining steps: turn left, walk straight to the pond.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child act out the full route first, then identify where the friend joins and repeat only the steps from that point; stretch: ask the child to write directions for a different route from the entry gate to the pond using different turns.

exercise.description: Follow the path Avi and Soni are following: walk on blue lane, turn right on green lane, take left towards red lane, take first left on golden lane, pass stalls to find the chaupal.

items.prompt: Anu and Bina both solved the same maze but wrote different lists of objects they found on the way. Anu found: snake, dog, pineapple. Bina found: dog, kite, star. What does this tell you about the maze? Give one reason.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The maze has more than one possible path. Anu and Bina took different routes to the exit, so they passed different objects along the way.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: If two people solve the same maze but encounter different objects, they must have followed different routes — which means at least two paths exist through the maze.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to think about whether two people could pass a snake and a star on exactly the same path — if not, their routes must differ; stretch: ask the child to describe what would need to be true about the maze for both Anu and Bina to encounter exactly the same objects.

exercise.description: Share the way you went through the maze. Write the things you found on the way.

items.section_title: Giant Wheel — Reading the Fair Map
items.prompt: A fair has symbols on its map for the following places: parking, ATM, restaurant, shops, giant wheel, pond, play area, and chaupal. How many different symbols are shown in the fair's map legend?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count each named place in the legend: parking, ATM, restaurant, shops, giant wheel, pond, play area, chaupal — eight in total.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child point to each place name in the legend list above and count aloud; stretch: ask the child to design a legend with two extra places of their own and say what symbol they would use for each.

exercise.description: How many exit routes are there in the fair?
